title: Active isolation of transmon readout with a tunable inductive bridge
authors: Chunyang Ding, Chuyao Tong, Paul Varosy, Nikitha Jain, Ziyi Zhao, Eric I. Rosenthal, Konrad W. Lehnert, David I. Schuster
abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum computation requires fast, high-fidelity readout. Currently, this is assisted through cryogenic amplification of the readout signal. In traditional dispersive readout schemes, the amplifiers that are used to provide high signal-to-noise ratio also generate thermal noise that can decohere the qubits, demanding additional ferrite-based isolators to suppress this noise. Here, we integrate a chip-scale microwave switch, the tunable inductive bridge, into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon. Flux-pulsing the switch, such that it transmits only during the readout, did not make a discernable difference to qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity metrics. By injecting broadband noise that mimics amplifier thermal photons, we show that the switch suppresses the resulting qubit dephasing by more than $30$~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio, establishing it as a potential chip-based integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators.
summary: This paper presents a tunable inductive bridge (TIB) as a compact, chip-scale replacement for traditional, bulky microwave isolators in superconducting quantum circuits. By demonstrating that the TIB can be pulsed to isolate the qubit during free evolution, the authors show it effectively suppresses thermal noise backaction from readout amplifiers by over 30 dB, paving the way for more scalable quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving fast, high-fidelity readout for scalable superconducting quantum computation while mitigating thermal noise backaction from necessary cryogenic amplifiers.
main_result: The tunable inductive bridge (TIB) successfully functions as a chip-scale, integrated replacement for bulky ferrite isolators, suppressing noise-induced qubit dephasing by over 30 dB without degrading qubit coherence.
method: The authors characterized the TIB by flux-pulsing it to transmit only during readout, and quantified noise suppression by injecting broadband thermal noise and measuring resulting qubit dephasing ($T_2^E$).
model_or_system: The experiment uses a fixed-frequency transmon qubit coupled to a readout resonator, with the TIB integrated into the readout chain. The system is analyzed by measuring coherence times and residual photon populations under pulsed vs. static operation.
key_observables: Readout fidelity (up to 99.82% pulsed), noise suppression ( $>30$ dB), qubit coherence times ($T_1, T_{2E}$), and residual excited-state population ($p_e$).
important_parameters: On/Off ratio (25–40 dB), noise suppression factor ($>30$ dB), and minimum detectable temperature ($\geq 84$ mK).
main_assumptions: The TIB's pulsed operation does not introduce measurable backaction thermal photons, and the injected noise spectrum serves as a good proxy for ambient thermal noise.
figures_summary: Figures characterize the TIB's transmission properties (on/off ratio, time response) and demonstrate noise suppression by comparing qubit echo oscillations ($T_2^E$) with and without injected noise.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for integrated isolators, then details the TIB's characterization (transmission, pulsing), followed by rigorous noise injection experiments to quantify noise suppression, and finally confirms coherence preservation across operational modes.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses hardware limitations in quantum computing by proposing a compact, tunable, and high-performance component to solve a critical noise mitigation problem in superconducting circuits.
